title: De‐Moralizing Friendship: Unfinished Business
abstract: We have duties to our friends that we don't have to strangers. Philosophers traditionally take these duties of friendship to be moral duties. But this moralist position cannot accommodate the full scope of the duties that we have to our friends. Many of these associative duties appear to be duties of a distinct normative kind. I defend a de‐moralized conception of friendship's distinctive reasons and obligations. On this framework, friendship constitutes a normative domain in its own right, distinct from the moral realm, and perhaps even the personal one; its concomitant duties can conflict with moral requirements as well as our self‐identifying commitments.

title: AI Death
abstract: This paper addresses the following questions: When do AIs die? Are AI labs or AI users causing the death of AIs? Is this bad for the AIs? What are our ethical responsibilities in light of the answers to these questions? It is currently unclear whether AIs are welfare subjects, and, if they are, whether their death is bad for them. But we argue that, if they are welfare subjects, today's AIs are plausibly dying all the time. If death is bad for AIs, the scale of the problem is daunting: as many as 1 billion AIs may die every day. We propose interventions for labs and users to avoid the risk of causing AI death.

title: Epistemological Casuistry: What's Not Wrong With Motivated Reasoning
abstract: We often accuse others, and sometimes ourselves, of engaging in, as psychologists are apt to term it, “motivated reasoning.” This is the charge that the collection, use, and interpretation of information have been warped by one'sdesires, andis often regarded as amounting to a charge of epistemic irrationality. In a 2015 paper in this journal, we appealed to this familiar charge of motivated reasoning to analyze the phenomenon of irrelevant influences on belief. There, we argued that motivated reasoning is indeed epistemically pernicious. Since then, a number of important objections have been made in different literatures. It has been argued that insofar as one's interests include defending one's prior beliefs, remaining internally coherent, defending one's social identity against threats from oppressive forces, or pursuing one's (otherwise reasonable) practical goals, such interests may permissibly influence reasoning, with no irrationality or “bad” reasoning implicated. In this paper, we address these recent objections and argue that, though the above points may illuminate important limitations of our original thesis, motivated reasoning is indeed a form of epistemic irrationality.

title: Urban Succession and Neighborhood Change
abstract: We argue the idea of “urban succession” provides an instructive lens through which to understand how cities change over time. We show how this model illuminates phenomena important to urban policymaking and reform, and we highlight several upshots that challenge conventional thinking about healthy cities’ constitutions. First, valuable urban conditions may be difficult or impossible to realize without allowing them to “grow” from prior conditions. Second, even when achieved, these conditions may be inherently unstable, predictably giving way to other conditions. Third, unwelcome urban phenomena can arise without being deliberately pursued and thus effective remedies must go beyond neutralizing or reforming the bad actors at the heart of theories from critical urban studies. Finally, when valuable urban conditions represent intermediate stages in succession‐like processes, this may illuminate new strategies for sustaining these conditions—as well as the folly of certain popular approaches to urban development, reform, and theorizing. We focus special attention on issues of gentrification and neighborhood decline, showing how our model helps contextualize these as predictable stages in long‐term processes of urban flux.

title: The Relational Risks of Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The increasingly widespread use of generative artificial intelligence has begun to reshape the landscape of interpersonal communication. It is no longer unusual, for example, for co‐workers to reply to each other's emails, or even romantic partners and family members to respond to each other with AI‐generated messages. Yet the suspicion that one has received AI‐generated, rather than human‐authored content is often accompanied by strong negative reactions ranging from disgust to disappointment. Focusing on the case of AI‐generated apologies, my paper systematically examines the moral reasons we typically appeal to for resenting someone who uses AI to convey an apology. Interestingly, these moral reasons do not decisively prohibit the use of generative AI in interpersonal communication. Rather, the emergent social practice of apologizing through AI poses a distinctive risk to interpersonal relations themselves. Chiefly, this practice threatens to degrade our ability to engage in careful “translation” of each other's linguistic performances, or conversely, enact “performance” in a way that can be taken up by the other (Brandom 1979, 190). This is because AI‐generated messages aim to “optimize” communication and minimize conflict and friction that, while not always pleasant, is vital to our understanding of, and responsiveness in relation to each other as authentic subjects. Consequently, closer attention must be paid to these relational risks of generative AI.

title: Responsibility as Personal Significance
abstract: This paper defends a view of what responsibility is, where responsibility is neither just the agential facts that make a person responsible, or is not the aptness of certain responses to those facts. Responsibility is the relevant agential facts, and the significance of those facts for the person. The fact that a person is responsible makes certain responses apt, and it grounds a range of other things, such as the person's duties and entitlements. But these are moral implications of being responsible; they are not constitutive of responsibility and they do not ground it. I have reason to care about whether my acts are mine as such, and not simply because of the implications of their being mine. Thus, responsibility matters in itself, independently of the responses that it is apt to make to it. This view can explain why ʻʻresponsibility’ is a thick normative term; why we appropriately use ʻʻresponsibility’ to refer to both positive and negative cases; why responsibility is unified, with a range of moral implications; and why we are responsible for trivial conduct that is not personally significant.

title: That's Not a Thing : Reification as a Tool for Ethical Critique
abstract: Reification is a social pathology that occurs when we treat social relations as things independent of our collective agency. It is not simply a category mistake, nor is it an isolated error that any single individual can correct. Rather, reification involves a collective and systematic reflexivity deficit caused by the unjust, oppressive, or unhealthy character of our social relations. In this paper, I present my own account of reification as a social pathology and demonstrate its uses—and potential abuses—for ethical critique. Reification distorts individual agency by obscuring our collective powers. I argue that the concept can play three roles in our analyses: diagnostic , etiological , and prescriptive . In relation to each of these functions, I show that the notion is both under‐ and overutilized. First, reification has yet to enter mainstream discourse in Anglophone moral and political philosophy, especially when compared with concepts of similar pedigree, such as ideology and alienation. I seek to rectify this neglect by showing that reification is a valuable addition to analyses of structural injustice, domination, value capture, and inauthenticity. Second, for critical theorists already immersed in historical debates over reification, I warn against the concept's overuse by more clearly circumscribing its critical reach. I propose ways to distinguish reification more carefully from objectification and commodification.

title: Normality in Action?
abstract: Recent years have seen an explosion of normality‐theoretic models of knowledge. At the same time, there has been renewed interest in the action‐guiding value of knowledge. The natural question that arises is whether knowledge, according to the normality‐framework, is action guiding. We consider putting the normality‐framework to good use in resolving thorny issues involving fanatical prospects. But ultimately, we give two arguments that suggest that whatever concept the normality framework is capturing (whether it really be knowledge or something else), it is not action‐guiding.

title: Inquiry and Logical Form
abstract: Joint inquiry requires agents to exchange public content about some target domain, which in turn requires them to track which content a linguistic form contributes to a conversation. But, often, the inquiry delivers a necessary truth. For example, if we are inquiring whether a particular bird, Tweety, is a woodpecker, and discover that it is, then our inquiry concluding in this fact would conclude in a necessity, and the form “Tweety is a woodpecker” expresses this necessary truth. Still, whether Tweety is a woodpecker seems a perfectly legitimate object of study, and the answers we accrue can be informative. But the dominant model of inquiry (Stalnaker, 1978, 1984) treats this situation as linguistically deviant, and diagnoses our ignorance and subsequent discovery as metalinguistic: we were ignorant, and ultimately discovered something, about the meaning of our terms. Rather than linguistic deviation, we argue this situation is the norm, and one that calls for an alternative model of inquiry. This paper develops such a model. It shows that to capture how agents can learn something informative about the world—and not merely language—even when inquiry concerns necessary facts, it's key to track how moves in discourse contribute public content onto the conversational record, but also, crucially, how those moves are connected by coherence relations to one another and to real‐world situations they are about. This allows us to capture that utterances contribute determinate, public content, while representing the information states of the interlocutors who may have only partial access to the evidence and content of the conversation, without making their ignorance metalinguistic. It lets us give precise explanations why some discourses can be transparently convincing in the conclusions they underwrite. The model thus precisifies the role of public context and shared content in anchoring an inquiry. It allows for imperfect tracking of linguistic contributions that are binding for how inquiry unfolds, and it allows for an inquiry into the status of necessary truths to be both informative, and involve empirical, rather than metalinguistic, ignorance.

title: Quantifiers for a Modal Future
abstract: Future auxiliaries present a challenge to the classical analysis of modal expressions as existential or universal quantifiers over a contextually provided set of possible worlds: these expressions come with a distinct modal flavor, but their interaction with negation and the fact that future judgments come in degrees of confidence is unexpected if the classical analysis were correct. I show how a uniform quantifier analysis of modal expressions can accommodate the distinct empirical phenomena surrounding future auxiliaries. The resulting analysis extends to address a set of related challenges that have been observed for a quantifier analysis of ability modals.
